title: Sustainable Agriculture Practices: Healthy Soil, Smart Water and Climate-Ready Farming
subtitle: Test your own soil and water, put proven low-cost practices to work, and prove with your own records that your land is getting healthier.
description: A practical course for women smallholders who want their land to keep producing. You will read your soil with home tests, rebuild fertility with compost, mulch and legumes, save water with pits, tanks and drip lines, manage pests safely with IPM, and run a fair trial that shows what works on your farm.
outcomes: Assess your soil texture, structure, water intake and soil life with simple home tests
Build compost, apply mulch and plan a four-season rotation that includes legumes
Calculate rainwater harvest and compare surface and drip irrigation water needs
Scout pests, decide when to act and follow recognised pesticide safety rules
Run a fair side-by-side trial and calculate yield per square metre and net gain
Present an honest project summary and a 90-day plan to extension officers or farmer groups
audience: Women who already farm a plot or field in Nigeria or elsewhere in Africa and want to stop soil decline, cope with erratic rain and cut input costs.
tools: A notebook and pen, or a notes app on your phone
A phone camera for dated photos
A clear plastic bottle or jar, a ruler and an empty tin with both ends removed
A spade or hoe, pegs and string
Buckets, gloves and access to crop residues, grass or manure
A weighing scale for harvests (a hanging scale works well)

modules.title: Reading Your Land: Soil, Water and Your Starting Point
modules.overview: Before changing anything, you learn what sustainable farming really protects and how to read your own field. You test your soil with simple tools, map your water and season, and finish with an honest baseline sheet that tells you which practice to start with.

lessons.title: What Sustainable Farming Protects: Soil Life, Nutrients and the Three Principles
objectives: Explain why yields fall on land that is farmed the same way every season
Describe the nutrient cycle on a small farm and where nutrients leave it
Name the three principles of conservation agriculture used by FAO
Recognise early signs that your soil is being run down

blocks.text: Sustainable agriculture means farming in a way that keeps your land able to feed you and earn for you next year, in ten years and when your children take over. It is not a special label or a costly system. It is a set of habits that **put back what each harvest takes out**, protect the soil from sun and rain, and use water carefully.

blocks.name: farming
blocks.alt: A farmer working in a green field
blocks.caption: Every practice in this course aims at one thing: a field that keeps producing season after season.

blocks.text: Why yields fall without any disaster

Every bag of maize, every basket of tomatoes and every heap of yams you carry away contains nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and other nutrients that came from your soil. When stalks are burnt and nothing is returned, the soil gets a little poorer each season. Rain then washes bare topsoil away, and the hot sun burns off the **organic matter**, the dark, crumbly remains of plants and animals that hold water and feed soil life. The result is a slow slide: more fertiliser for the same harvest, harder ground, and crops that wilt quickly in a dry spell.

Soil is alive. A handful of healthy soil holds earthworms, termites, fungi and billions of bacteria. Some bacteria, called **rhizobia**, live in small lumps (nodules) on the roots of legumes such as cowpea, groundnut and soybean, and turn nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use. Fungi spread thin threads that help roots reach water and phosphorus. When you feed and protect this underground workforce, it works for you for free.

Sustainable farming also looks beyond the soil. It protects water by stopping runoff and wasteful irrigation, protects the insects and birds that pollinate crops and eat pests, and protects your family by cutting careless pesticide use. On a small farm these goals usually point the same way: a covered, living soil holds more rain, grows stronger plants and needs fewer costly rescues.

blocks.title: The nutrient cycle on a small farm
items: Soil feeds the crop
Harvest leaves the farm
Residues and manure return
Soil life breaks them down
Nutrients ready again
blocks.caption: Nutrients only stay in the cycle if residues, manure and compost go back; burning or removing everything breaks the loop.

blocks.text: The three principles of conservation agriculture

The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) describes conservation agriculture with three linked principles. You do not need to adopt all of them at once, but they explain why the practices in Module 2 work.

head: Principle
What it means on your farm
Simple ways to start
rows: Dig and plough only where and when you must, so soil structure and soil life are not destroyed
Plant in rows or holes instead of turning the whole field; avoid burning before planting
Keep the ground covered by crops, crop residues or mulch for most of the year
Leave maize stalks or grass mulch on the surface; grow a cover crop after harvest
Grow different crop families in rotation or together
Follow maize with cowpea or groundnut; intercrop cassava with a legume

blocks.title: Sustainable does not mean no fertiliser
blocks.text: Many poor soils in Nigeria need some mineral fertiliser to give a decent yield. Sustainable farming uses compost, legumes and mulch so that every bag of fertiliser you buy works harder and less is wasted. The aim is healthy soil and a fair profit, not a slogan.
Early warning signs on your land

items: A hard crust forms on the surface after rain and seedlings struggle to push through
Rainwater runs off in brown streams instead of soaking in, leaving small gullies
The topsoil is pale and powdery rather than dark and crumbly
You rarely see earthworms or their small soil castings when you dig
You need more fertiliser each year to get the same harvest
Crops wilt within a few days of a dry spell while a neighbour's mulched field stays green

blocks.title: Worked example: is the soil being run down?
blocks.context: For example, Amina farms 1 hectare of maize near Zaria. She burns the stalks every dry season and writes down her fertiliser and harvest each year.
steps: Year 1: she used 4 bags (50 kg each) of NPK and harvested 40 bags (100 kg each) of maize. That is 40 divided by 4 = 10 bags of maize for each bag of fertiliser.
Year 4: she used 6 bags of NPK and harvested 36 bags of maize. That is 36 divided by 6 = 6 bags of maize for each bag of fertiliser.
The return on each bag of fertiliser fell from 10 to 6, a drop of 40 percent, even though she spent more.
Rainfall in both years was normal, so the weather does not explain the drop. Burnt residues, bare soil and no legumes are the likely causes.
blocks.result: Amina's own records show her soil is getting poorer. Her first targets are to stop burning stalks, keep them as mulch and bring cowpea into the rotation, then track the same two numbers next season.

blocks.text: Notice that Amina did not need a laboratory to see the problem. Two numbers written down each year, fertiliser used and harvest, told the story. You will build this habit of simple records throughout the course, because sustainable practices prove themselves slowly and only records show the change.

takeaways: Each harvest removes nutrients; residues, manure and compost put them back
Soil life, including rhizobia and fungi, does free work when protected
FAO's three principles: minimum disturbance, permanent cover, crop diversity
Track fertiliser used and harvest each season to see if soil is improving or declining

activity.title: Your two-number soil check
steps: Write down, for your main crop, how much fertiliser you used last season and how much you harvested
If you remember an earlier season, write the same two numbers for that year
Divide harvest by fertiliser for each season and compare the results
Walk your field and tick any of the six warning signs you can see
Write one sentence: is my soil improving, steady or declining, and why do I think so?
activity.evidence: A notebook page with your numbers, your ticked warning signs and your one-sentence judgement

lessons.title: Testing Your Soil at Home: Texture, Structure, Water Intake and pH
objectives: Identify your soil texture using the feel test and the jar test
Measure how fast water soaks into your soil with a simple tin test
Count earthworms as a quick sign of soil life
Decide when a laboratory soil test is worth paying for

blocks.text: General advice such as "add compost" or "irrigate twice a week" only helps if it fits your soil. A sandy soil drains fast and dries out; a clay soil holds water but can become waterlogged and hard. In this lesson you test your own soil with a bottle, a tin, a ruler and your hands. Do the tests at three or four spots in your field, because soil can change from the top of a slope to the bottom.

blocks.name: environmental-study
blocks.caption: Simple home tests tell you most of what you need to know about your soil before spending money.

blocks.text: Test 1: texture by feel

Soil is made of three sizes of mineral particles. **Sand** is the largest and feels gritty. **Silt** is medium and feels smooth like flour. **Clay** is the finest and feels sticky when wet. The mix of the three is called **texture**, and it decides how well soil holds water and nutrients.

items: Take a small handful of soil from about 15 cm deep and remove stones and roots.
Add water drop by drop and knead until it feels like soft dough.
Squeeze it between thumb and finger, pushing it upwards to make a ribbon.
No ribbon and very gritty: sandy soil. Short ribbon under 2.5 cm: loam. Ribbon 2.5 to 5 cm: clay loam. Long ribbon over 5 cm that is sticky: clay.
Rub a wet pinch in your palm: gritty means more sand, smooth means more silt, sticky means more clay.

blocks.text: Test 2: the jar test

Fill a clear straight-sided bottle or jar about one third with soil. Add water until it is about three quarters full, add a teaspoon of powdered detergent or a few drops of dish soap to help the particles separate, close it and shake hard for three minutes. Set it down where it will not be moved. Sand settles in about one minute, silt within a few hours, and clay can take one or two days. Then measure each layer with a ruler.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a jar test
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma in Nsukka shakes soil from her vegetable plot in a clear bottle and measures the layers after two days.
steps: Bottom layer (sand): 3.0 cm. Middle layer (silt): 1.5 cm. Top layer (clay): 1.0 cm. Total: 5.5 cm.
Sand: 3.0 divided by 5.5 = 0.545, about 55 percent.
Silt: 1.5 divided by 5.5 = 0.273, about 27 percent.
Clay: 1.0 divided by 5.5 = 0.182, about 18 percent.
On the standard soil texture triangle, about 55 percent sand, 27 percent silt and 18 percent clay falls in the sandy loam class.
blocks.result: Ifeoma has a sandy loam: easy to work and well drained, but it dries quickly and loses nutrients to heavy rain. Mulch and compost will be her most valuable practices.

blocks.text: Test 3: how fast water soaks in

Remove both ends from a tin such as a tomato paste or milk tin. Push it about 5 cm into moist soil. Pour in water to a level 2.5 cm deep (mark the level inside first) and time how long it takes to disappear. Do it twice in the same spot and use the second time, because the first pour wets dry soil. If water vanishes in a few minutes, the soil drains fast and dries out quickly. If it takes over an hour, the surface is sealed or compacted and rain will run off instead of soaking in. Compare a spot in your field with a spot under a tree or in an old fallow: the difference shows what better soil cover could do.
Test 4: structure and soil life

Dig a block of soil one spade wide and one spade deep, about 20 cm. Break it gently. Good structure crumbles into rounded crumbs of different sizes with many pores and roots. Poor structure comes out as hard flat plates or as loose dust. Now count the earthworms in that block. Many soil guides treat about ten or more earthworms in a spade-sized block as a sign of active soil life, but numbers drop in very dry or very wet weather, so compare spots on the same day and repeat in the same month next year.

blocks.title: Your soil walk checklist
items: Texture by feel
Jar test layers
Water intake time
Crumb structure
Earthworm count
Surface crust or erosion
blocks.caption: Record all six at each test spot so next year's walk can be compared like for like.

blocks.text: Soil pH and when to pay for a lab test

Soil pH measures acidity. Most food crops grow best between about **pH 5.5 and 7.0**. Many soils in humid southern Nigeria are acidic, which locks up phosphorus and can hold back crops even when you add fertiliser. Signs include poor growth despite fertiliser and plants that do better near old ash heaps. Cheap pH test strips and kits exist, but they are rough guides. A laboratory test also reports organic carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, and gives a fertiliser and lime recommendation.

blocks.title: Where to get a soil test
blocks.text: Ask your state Agricultural Development Programme (ADP) office, a nearby federal or state university with a soil science department, or an agricultural research institute. Prices vary widely, so ask for the price per sample before you send it. One mixed sample made from 10 to 15 small scoops taken in a zig-zag across one field is better than a single scoop.

blocks.title: Careful with lime and ash
blocks.text: Agricultural lime and wood ash both reduce acidity, but too much can push pH too high and lock up other nutrients. Apply lime only on the advice of a soil test, wear gloves and a dust mask when spreading it, and keep it away from children.

takeaways: Texture (sand, silt, clay) decides how your soil holds water and nutrients
The jar test turns layer heights into percentages you can read on the texture triangle
A tin and a watch show whether rain soaks in or runs off
Crumb structure and earthworms are quick signs of living soil
Pay for a lab test before liming or when fertiliser stops working

activity.title: Do a full soil walk
steps: Choose three spots in your field: top, middle and bottom of any slope
Do the feel test and the tin water-intake test at each spot
Do one jar test with a mixed sample and work out the percentages
Dig one spade block per spot, describe the structure and count earthworms
Record everything in a table with the date and the weather of the past week
activity.evidence: A photo of your settled jar with a ruler beside it and your completed soil walk table

lessons.title: Mapping Water, Season and Resources: Your Farm Baseline and Priority
objectives: Map every water source on or near your farm and how reliable it is
Use the NiMet seasonal prediction to plan planting dates
Rate possible practices by cost, labour and impact
Choose one priority problem and the practice you will start with

blocks.text: Your soil walk showed what is under your feet. Now map what comes from above and around: water, season length, labour and money. Together they make your **baseline**, the honest picture of your farm today that every later improvement is measured against.

blocks.name: weather-forecast
blocks.alt: A person checking a weather forecast
blocks.caption: Knowing when the rains are expected to start and stop shapes every planting decision.

blocks.text: Map your water

Draw a simple sketch of your farm in your notebook. Mark the slope (which way water runs after rain), any stream, well, borehole, pond or roof that could supply water, and how far each is from your plots. Next to each source write when it dries up. A stream that flows only from June to October is very different from a borehole you can use all year. Note who else depends on the same source, because shared water needs agreement before you plan dry-season vegetables around it.
Know your season

Most Nigerian farming is rain-fed, so the start (onset), end (cessation) and length of the rainy season decide which varieties will finish before the soil dries. Each year the **Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet)** publishes a **Seasonal Climate Prediction (SCP)** with expected onset and cessation dates, season length and possible dry spells for different parts of the country. Your ADP extension officer and many farmer groups share it. Use it together with your own experience: planting after the first single heavy shower, before the rains are steady, is a common way to lose seed.

blocks.title: Keep a rain gauge
blocks.text: A straight-sided tin or plastic container with a flat bottom left in the open works as a simple rain gauge. After each rain, measure the depth of water in millimetres with a ruler, write it down with the date, then empty it. One season of records tells you more about your own farm than any national average.
Count your other resources

Practices differ in what they demand. Crop rotation and seed saving cost mainly planning. Composting and mulching cost labour and access to plant material or manure. A drip kit or water tank costs cash. Write down honestly: how many days a week you and your household can give to the farm, what organic material you can get (crop residues, grass, animal manure, market waste), and what money you could spend this season.

Also note how secure your access to the land is. If you rent a plot for one season at a time, quick practices such as mulch, legumes and planting pits pay back within the season and make sense. Planting trees or building a large compost site makes more sense on land you expect to farm for several years, or where you have a written agreement with the owner or family head. Many women farm land held by a husband or extended family, so talk early with whoever decides, and show them the plan and the expected benefit before you change how the field is used.

head: Practice
Main cost
Labour
When results show
rows: Stop burning, keep residues as mulch
First dry spell, more over 2 to 3 seasons
After 2 to 3 months, builds over years

blocks.title: Choosing where to start
items: Quick wins: low cost, high impact
Plan and save: high cost, high impact
Easy extras: low cost, low impact
Avoid for now: high cost, low impact
blocks.caption: Start in the quick-win corner for your main problem, then plan the bigger investments.

blocks.title: Worked example: scoring practices for one farm
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa grows maize and soybean on 0.5 hectare near Kaduna. Her soil walk showed a sandy loam with a hard crust and slow water intake, and two dry spells hurt her maize last year. She has little cash but her family can help two days a week.
steps: Her main problem: rain runs off and the crop suffers in dry spells.
She scores each practice from 1 (poor) to 3 (good) on cost, labour and impact on that problem.
Residue mulch: cost 3, labour 3, impact 3 = 9 points.
Tied ridges: cost 3, labour 1, impact 3 = 7 points.
Composting: cost 2, labour 1, impact 2 = 5 points.
Drip kit: cost 1, labour 3, impact 1 (she has no dry-season water source) = 5 points.
blocks.result: Hauwa starts with residue mulch on the whole field (9 points) and tests tied ridges on one quarter of it. Composting waits until she has more help.

blocks.text: Your readiness checklist

items: I know my soil texture, water intake time and structure at three spots
I have a sketch of my farm showing slope and every water source
I know this year's expected onset and cessation dates for my area
I have listed the labour, materials and cash I can really use this season
I have named one main problem and one practice to start with
I know one nearby farmer or extension worker I can ask for advice

takeaways: Your baseline covers soil, water, season, labour, materials and money
NiMet's Seasonal Climate Prediction and your own rain records guide planting dates
Score practices by cost, labour and impact on your main problem
Start with one quick-win practice and test bigger changes on part of the field

activity.title: Write your farm baseline sheet
steps: Draw your farm sketch with slope, plots and water sources, and note when each source dries up
Find this year's NiMet onset and cessation dates for your state from your ADP or a farmer group
List the labour days, organic materials and cash you can use this season
Score at least four practices from the table on cost, labour and impact
Circle your main problem and your chosen first practice
activity.evidence: One baseline sheet (photo or paper) with the sketch, season dates, resource list and practice scores

quiz.q: Amina used 4 bags of fertiliser for 40 bags of maize in one year and 6 bags for 36 bags of maize three years later, with normal rain both years. What does this most likely show?
options: Her soil is getting poorer and each bag of fertiliser is doing less
She simply needs to double her fertiliser
quiz.explain: Harvest per bag of fertiliser fell from 10 to 6 with normal rain, a classic sign of declining soil organic matter and nutrient loss.

quiz.q: A jar test shows sand 2 cm, silt 2 cm and clay 1 cm. What percentage is clay?
quiz.explain: Total height is 5 cm. Clay is 1 divided by 5 = 0.2, which is 20 percent.

quiz.q: In the tin test, the second pour of 2.5 cm of water takes more than an hour to soak in. What does this tell her?
options: The soil is very sandy and drains too fast
The surface is sealed or compacted, so rain will tend to run off
The soil pH is too high
quiz.explain: Very slow intake means water cannot enter the soil easily, so rain runs off. Soil cover and less disturbance help.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of FAO's three principles of conservation agriculture?
quiz.explain: Burning removes soil cover and organic matter. The three principles are minimum disturbance, permanent cover and crop diversification.

quiz.q: Hauwa has little cash, no dry-season water and a crusting soil that loses rain as runoff. Which first practice fits best?
options: Keeping crop residues on the surface as mulch
Liming the whole farm without a soil test
Planting before the first steady rains
quiz.explain: Residue mulch costs almost nothing, reduces crusting and runoff and keeps moisture in during dry spells. Drip needs a water source she does not have.

modules.title: Field Practices: Feeding Soil, Saving Water and Managing Pests Safely
modules.overview: This module is hands-on. You make compost and mulch, plan a legume rotation, capture and stretch water with pits, ridges, tanks and drip lines, and manage pests with scouting and integrated pest management, using chemicals only safely and as a last step.

lessons.title: Building Soil Fertility: Compost, Mulch, Legumes and Crop Rotation
objectives: Build a compost heap with the right mix of green and brown materials
Calculate how much compost a vegetable bed needs
Apply mulch correctly around crops
Plan a crop rotation that brings legumes into every cycle

blocks.text: Module 1 showed you whether your soil is losing ground. This lesson gives you four low-cost tools to rebuild it: **compost**, **mulch**, **legumes** and **rotation**. None of them needs a shop. They need planning, some labour and the plant material and manure that are already around most farms.

blocks.name: gardening
blocks.alt: A woman tending plants in a garden bed
blocks.caption: Compost, mulch and legumes turn farm waste into fertility that stays in your soil.

blocks.text: Making compost that works

Compost is plant and animal waste that soil organisms have broken down into a dark, crumbly material. It feeds soil life, slowly releases nutrients and helps sandy soil hold water and clay soil drain. A good heap balances two kinds of material. **Greens** are fresh and rich in nitrogen: fresh leaves, vegetable peels, fresh grass, and poultry, goat or cow manure. **Browns** are dry and rich in carbon: dry maize stalks cut short, dry leaves, straw, rice husks and sawdust from untreated wood. A common guide is about two to three parts browns to one part greens by volume.

items: Choose a shaded spot near water. In dry areas dig a pit about 50 cm deep; in wet areas build a heap on the ground so it does not waterlog.
Lay a base of coarse sticks or stalks about 15 cm deep so air can enter from below.
Add layers: about 15 to 20 cm of browns, then 5 to 10 cm of greens and manure, then a thin sprinkle of old soil or compost to bring in soil organisms.
Water each layer until it is moist like a squeezed-out sponge, not dripping.
Build it to about 1 m wide and 1 m high so it can heat up, then cover with leaves, sacks or old roofing sheet against sun and heavy rain.
After a week, push a stick or cutlass into the centre for a minute. It should come out warm. Turn the heap every one to two weeks, moving outside material to the middle and adding water if dry.
Compost is ready when it is dark and crumbly, smells of earth and you can no longer recognise the starting materials, often after about two to three months with regular turning in warm weather.

blocks.title: Handling manure and compost safely
blocks.text: Manure can carry germs that cause illness. Wear gloves or wash hands well with soap after handling it, and keep cuts covered. Never use human, dog or cat faeces. Use only well-made compost or well-rotted manure on vegetables eaten raw, and do not add meat, bones, oily food, plastic or diseased plants to the heap.

blocks.title: Worked example: how much compost for a vegetable bed?
blocks.context: For example, Blessing in Ibadan has a raised bed 1.2 m wide and 8 m long for tomatoes. Her extension officer suggests working about 3 cm of compost into the top of the bed before planting.
steps: Bed area: 1.2 m x 8 m = 9.6 square metres.
Compost depth: 3 cm = 0.03 m.
Volume: 9.6 x 0.03 = 0.288 cubic metres. One cubic metre is 1,000 litres, so she needs about 288 litres.
In 20-litre buckets: 288 divided by 20 = 14.4, so about 15 buckets.
A fresh heap 1.5 m x 1.5 m x 1 m holds 2.25 cubic metres of material. Heaps commonly shrink to about half as they decompose, leaving roughly 1.1 cubic metres, about 1,100 litres.
blocks.result: One well-built heap gives Blessing about 1,100 litres, enough for 1,100 divided by 288 = about 3.8 beds of this size. She plans one heap for every three to four beds.

blocks.text: Mulch: a blanket for your soil

Mulch is any material laid on the soil surface: dry grass, maize or sorghum stalks, rice straw, leaves or groundnut haulms. It shades the soil, stops raindrops from smashing the surface into a crust, slows evaporation, keeps roots cooler and smothers many weeds. As it breaks down it feeds soil life. Spread a layer about 5 to 10 cm thick after the soil is moist, and keep it a few centimetres away from plant stems to prevent rot. Termites may eat some mulch in dry areas; that is normal, but top it up and keep it away from young stems.
Legumes and rotation

Legumes such as cowpea, groundnut, soybean, bambara nut and pigeon pea carry rhizobia in root nodules that fix nitrogen from the air. Cut a healthy nodule open during flowering: pink or red inside means it is actively fixing nitrogen. Growing a legume before or alongside a cereal can reduce the nitrogen the cereal needs from fertiliser, especially when legume leaves and haulms are returned to the soil. Cover crops such as mucuna (velvet bean) or lablab can also be grown after the main crop or in a fallow to cover the soil, add organic matter and suppress weeds.

Rotation means changing the crop family on each plot each season. It breaks the life cycles of pests and diseases that attack one family, and different crops take nutrients from different depths. A key rule: do not follow tomato with pepper, garden egg or Irish potato, because they belong to the same family and share diseases such as bacterial wilt.

blocks.title: A four-season rotation for one plot
items: Cereal: maize or sorghum
Legume: cowpea or groundnut
Fruit vegetable: tomato or pepper
Leaf or root crop
blocks.caption: Each plot moves one step each season, so no crop family follows itself and every cycle includes a nitrogen-fixing legume.

head: Crop family
Nigerian examples
Notes for rotation
rows: Heavy nitrogen users; plant after a legume
Fix nitrogen; return haulms or leaves to the soil
Tomato, pepper, garden egg, Irish potato
Never follow each other; share wilt diseases
Long season; intercrop with a legume early on

takeaways: Compost needs browns and greens, air, moisture and turning; a hot centre means it is working
Volume needed equals area times depth; 1 cubic metre is 1,000 litres
Mulch 5 to 10 cm thick protects soil and saves water; keep it off stems
Rotate crop families and include a legume in every cycle

activity.title: Start a heap and plan your rotation
steps: List the green and brown materials you can collect in the next two weeks
Build a compost heap or pit following the steps and note the date
Check the centre temperature with a stick after one week and record it as cold, warm or hot
Draw your plots and write which crop family goes on each plot for the next four seasons
Calculate how many buckets of compost one of your beds or plots needs
activity.evidence: A dated photo of your compost heap and your four-season rotation plan with the compost calculation

lessons.title: Saving Water: Mulch, Planting Pits, Rainwater Tanks and Drip Irrigation
objectives: Choose water-harvesting methods that fit your rainfall and slope
Calculate how much rainwater a roof can collect
Compare the water needed by surface and drip irrigation
Check soil moisture by hand before watering

blocks.text: Water problems on small farms come in two forms. In the rainy season, rain falls hard and runs off before it soaks in. In dry spells and the dry season, there is not enough water and what there is gets wasted. The answer is to **catch rain where it falls, keep it in the soil, and deliver irrigation only where roots can use it**.

blocks.name: watering-plants
blocks.caption: Every litre that reaches the roots instead of running off or evaporating is a litre saved.

blocks.text: Catch rain in the field

items: **Planting pits (zai pits):** a traditional Sahel technique. Dig pits roughly 20 to 40 cm across and 10 to 20 cm deep, put a handful or two of compost or manure in each and plant in them. They collect runoff and concentrate nutrients around the roots, and are most useful on crusted, degraded soils in drier areas.
**Half-moons:** crescent-shaped earth bunds, open side facing uphill, that trap water running down a gentle slope. Plant inside the curve.
**Tied ridges:** ordinary ridges with small cross-ties every few metres, making a grid of basins that hold rain in place instead of letting it flow down the furrow.
**Contour planting:** ridges, rows and grass strips laid across the slope, never up and down it, so water slows and soaks in.
**Mulch and residues:** from the last lesson, they cut crusting and evaporation at almost no cost.

blocks.text: Store water from roofs

A useful fact: **1 mm of rain on 1 square metre gives 1 litre of water**. Multiply the roof area by the rainfall in millimetres, then by a runoff factor of about 0.8 for a metal roof, because some water splashes, evaporates or is lost in gutters. Fit a mesh at the tank inlet and divert the first few minutes of each rain away from the tank, since it carries dust and droppings from the roof.

blocks.title: Worked example: tank or drip, how far will the water go?
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Jos has a metal roof 6 m by 8 m, a 1,000-litre tank and a 100 square metre tomato plot for the dry season. For this example, her extension officer estimates the crop needs about 4 mm of water a day at its peak.
steps: Roof area: 6 x 8 = 48 square metres. One 25 mm rain gives 48 x 25 x 0.8 = 960 litres, so one good rain nearly fills the tank.
Net water the crop needs: 4 mm x 100 square metres = 400 litres per day.
FAO training manuals use indicative field application efficiencies of about 60 percent for surface irrigation and 90 percent for drip.
Surface or watering can: 400 divided by 0.60 = about 667 litres per day.
Drip: 400 divided by 0.90 = about 444 litres per day, a saving of about 222 litres every day (666.7 minus 444.4).
Over 60 days of peak demand, drip saves about 222 x 60 = 13,320 litres.
blocks.result: A full tank covers just over 2 days of drip irrigation at peak. Grace uses the tank for her nursery and early weeks, and plans a borehole share or shallow well for the full dry-season crop, with drip lines to make that water go further.

blocks.title: Surface watering versus drip
items: Surface or watering can
Drip lines
blocks.caption: Drip costs more to set up but stretches scarce water much further and saves carrying time.

blocks.text: Small drip systems

A family drip kit is a tank raised on a stand about 1 m or more above the bed, a filter, a main pipe and thin drip lines with small emitters beside each plant. Gravity does the work, so no pump or power is needed. Clean the filter every few days, flush the line ends weekly, and check that each emitter drips, because blocked emitters are the most common reason a crop dries out unevenly. Lay mulch over the lines to cut evaporation further.
Water at the right time and amount

items: Dig with a finger or stick to the root zone, about 10 to 15 cm deep for vegetables.
Squeeze a handful. If it holds together and leaves your hand slightly damp, there is enough water. If it crumbles and feels dry, water now.
Water early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when less is lost to evaporation and wind.
Water the soil at the base of the plant, not the leaves, which also reduces leaf diseases.
Water deeply and less often rather than a light splash every day, so roots grow down.

blocks.title: Water, mosquitoes and children
blocks.text: Cover every tank, drum and pot of stored water with a tight lid or mesh so mosquitoes cannot breed in it. Fence or cover open ponds and deep pits and never leave children alone near them. Do not use untreated sewage or drainage water on vegetables eaten raw, because it can carry germs that cause serious illness.

takeaways: Catch rain where it falls with pits, half-moons, tied ridges and contour rows
Roof harvest in litres = area in square metres x rain in mm x about 0.8
Drip delivers about 90 percent of water to roots against about 60 percent for surface watering
Check moisture by hand and water deeply in the cool part of the day

activity.title: Your water plan
steps: Measure your roof or any surface you could harvest from and calculate the litres from a 20 mm rain
Choose one in-field method (pits, tied ridges, half-moons or contour rows) for one plot and mark where it will go
Do the hand squeeze test on one plot on three days and write what you found
Estimate your daily watering need and compare surface and drip using the 60 and 90 percent figures
activity.evidence: Your water calculations and a sketch or photo of the plot where you will try one water-harvesting method

lessons.title: Integrated Pest Management and Safe Pesticide Use
objectives: Scout a field and calculate the percentage of damaged plants
Use prevention, natural enemies and push-pull before chemicals
Identify fall armyworm damage on maize
Follow recognised safety rules if a pesticide is needed

blocks.text: **Integrated pest management (IPM)** means using several methods together to keep pests below the level that costs you money, while protecting your health, beneficial insects and the soil. It replaces spraying on a fixed calendar with a simple routine: prevent, watch, decide, then act with the least harmful option that works.

blocks.name: lady-beetle
blocks.caption: Ladybirds and their larvae eat aphids; careless spraying kills these free helpers first.

blocks.title: The IPM pyramid
items: Prevention: healthy soil, rotation, clean seed
Scouting and records
Physical and biological control
Targeted pesticide, last resort
blocks.caption: Most of the work sits at the wide base; chemicals belong at the narrow top and only when scouting shows they are needed.

blocks.text: Step 1: prevent

items: Rotate crop families so pests and diseases cannot build up in the same plot
Use certified or well-selected clean seed and resistant varieties where available
Plant at the right time and spacing; stressed, crowded plants attract pests
Remove and destroy badly diseased plants and crop debris that carry pests between seasons
Keep field edges with flowering plants that shelter ladybirds, hoverflies and parasitic wasps

blocks.text: Step 2: scout and measure

Walk the field once or twice a week in a W pattern, stopping at five places away from the edge. At each stop check a fixed number of plants, for example 20, and count those with fresh damage or live pests. Record the date and the count. The percentage tells you whether the problem is growing, and comparing with your extension officer's advice tells you when to act.
Know your enemy: fall armyworm

Fall armyworm, a caterpillar originally from the Americas, was first reported in West and Central Africa in 2016, including Nigeria, and now attacks maize in most seasons. Look for small windowpane patches on young leaves, ragged holes, and wet sawdust-like droppings (frass) in the funnel (whorl) of the plant. The larva has a pale upside-down Y on its head and four dark dots forming a square near its tail end. Young larvae are easiest to control, so early scouting matters.

blocks.title: Worked example: to act or to wait?
blocks.context: For example, Bisi grows 0.5 hectare of maize in Oyo State. Her ADP officer advised her to take action against fall armyworm if fresh whorl damage passes 20 percent of young plants. This action level is an example; ask your own officer for advice for your crop and stage.
steps: Week 3 after planting: 5 stops x 20 plants = 100 plants checked. 12 have fresh damage: 12 divided by 100 = 12 percent.
Below 20 percent, so she crushes egg masses and young larvae by hand on damaged plants and scouts again in 4 days.
Week 4: 100 plants checked, 27 with fresh damage = 27 percent, now above the action level.
She chooses a targeted option recommended by her officer and registered for maize, applied into the whorls of affected areas rather than blanket spraying the whole field.
Week 5: fresh damage falls to 8 percent, so she returns to scouting only.
blocks.result: Bisi treated once, at the right time and in the right place, instead of spraying every week. She saved money and protected the natural enemies that keep pests down between treatments.

blocks.text: Step 3: physical and biological options

Hand-picking, removing infested plant parts and traps work well on small plots. **Push-pull**, developed by icipe (the International Centre of Insect Physiology and Ecology) with partners, plants the legume Desmodium between maize rows to push stemborer moths and fall armyworm away, and a border of Napier or Brachiaria grass to pull them out of the crop. Desmodium also suppresses the parasitic Striga weed and adds nitrogen. Botanical sprays such as neem seed extract are widely used by smallholders; a common recipe soaks about 50 g of ground neem seed kernels per litre of water overnight, then filters it. Botanicals are milder, but still wear gloves and wash hands after use.
Step 4: if you must use a pesticide

blocks.title: Recognised pesticide safety rules
blocks.text: Buy only from a registered agro-dealer, in the original sealed container with a NAFDAC registration number on the label. Read the label: which crop and pest it is approved for, the protective clothing needed, the re-entry interval and the pre-harvest interval (days to wait before harvest). Never mix or exceed the label rate. Wear gloves, long sleeves, trousers, boots and eye protection; spray in calm, cool weather, never into the wind; do not eat, drink or smoke while working, and wash well afterwards. Pregnant or breastfeeding women and children should not mix or spray. Store pesticides locked away from food, water and children, never in drink bottles. Triple-rinse empty containers into the sprayer, puncture them and never reuse them for food or water. If someone feels ill after exposure, go to a health facility at once and take the label with you.

Keep a spray record: date, product, plot, amount mixed, weather and the date when harvest is safe. Buyers and food processors increasingly ask about pesticide use, and the record protects you if a question about residues ever comes up.

takeaways: IPM order: prevent, scout, physical and biological control, then targeted chemicals
Scout fixed numbers of plants at five stops and work out the percentage damaged
Fall armyworm: windowpane feeding, frass in the whorl, Y on head, four dots near tail
Push-pull with Desmodium and Napier or Brachiaria reduces stemborers, armyworm and Striga
Read and follow the label, wear protection and respect the pre-harvest interval

activity.title: Run a scouting week
steps: Walk your main crop field in a W pattern and check 20 plants at each of five stops
Record the number of damaged plants and calculate the percentage
Photograph any pest or damage you cannot identify and ask your extension officer or farmer group
Repeat after four days and decide: wait, act by hand, or seek a targeted treatment
If you hold any pesticide at home, check its label, storage and container against the safety rules
activity.evidence: Your two-visit scouting record with percentages, your decision and photos of the pests or damage found

quiz.q: A compost heap smells bad and feels slimy. Which fix is most likely to help?
options: Add more fresh green leaves and manure
Add dry browns such as chopped stalks and turn it to let air in
Cover it with plastic so it stays wet
Leave it untouched for six months
quiz.explain: A slimy, smelly heap usually has too much wet green material and too little air. Dry browns and turning restore the balance.

quiz.q: A bed is 1 m wide and 10 m long. How many 20-litre buckets are needed for a 2 cm layer of compost?
quiz.explain: Area 10 square metres x 0.02 m = 0.2 cubic metres = 200 litres. 200 divided by 20 = 10 buckets.

quiz.q: A crop needs 300 litres of water a day at the roots. Using FAO's indicative efficiencies, about how much must be applied by drip?
quiz.explain: Drip is about 90 percent efficient: 300 divided by 0.9 = about 333 litres. Surface watering at 60 percent would need 500 litres.

quiz.q: Last season Kemi grew tomatoes on plot A. Which crop is the poorest choice for plot A this season?
quiz.explain: Pepper is in the same family as tomato and shares diseases such as bacterial wilt, so it should not follow tomato.

quiz.q: Scouting finds 9 of 100 maize plants with fresh fall armyworm damage. Her officer's action level is 20 percent. What should she do next?
options: Spray the whole field today to be safe
Hand-crush egg masses and young larvae and scout again in a few days
Ignore the field for the rest of the season
Burn the damaged plants and replant the field
quiz.explain: Damage is 9 percent, below the action level. IPM says use physical control and keep monitoring rather than spraying.

options: Checking the pre-harvest interval on the label
Storing leftover pesticide in a clean drink bottle in the kitchen
Spraying in calm, cool morning weather
Triple-rinsing and puncturing an empty container
quiz.explain: Pesticide in a drink bottle near food is a well-known cause of poisoning, especially of children. Keep it in the original labelled container, locked away.

modules.title: Climate-Smart Choices, Proof and Community Leadership
modules.overview: Now you prove what works on your own land and share it. You choose climate-smart options, run a fair side-by-side trial with simple records, work with extension services and farmer groups, and finish with a documented project and a 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Climate-Smart Choices and Running a Fair On-Farm Trial
objectives: Explain the three goals of climate-smart agriculture
Choose varieties, timing and tree options that reduce climate risk
Set up a fair side-by-side trial that tests one change at a time
Calculate yield per square metre and the net gain from a practice

blocks.text: Rainfall in many parts of Nigeria is becoming harder to predict: late onsets, long dry spells in the middle of the season and heavy storms that wash soil away. **Climate-smart agriculture**, as FAO describes it, has three goals: raise productivity and incomes sustainably, help farms adapt and recover from climate shocks, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions where possible. On a small farm the first two come first, and the practices you learned in Module 2 already serve both.

blocks.name: growth-chart
blocks.alt: A person beside a rising chart
blocks.caption: A fair trial and honest records turn a hopeful practice into proof you can show others.

blocks.text: Climate-smart options to consider

items: **Drought-tolerant and early-maturing varieties:** research centres such as IITA have worked with national partners to release maize and cowpea varieties that cope better with dry spells or finish before the rains end. Ask your ADP or a registered seed company which certified varieties suit your zone.
**Planting dates from the forecast:** use NiMet's Seasonal Climate Prediction and your rain gauge to plant once the rains are established, and stagger plantings a week or two apart to spread risk.

**Trees on the farm (agroforestry):** boundary trees and windbreaks reduce wind damage and drying. In the drier north, Faidherbia albida is valued because it drops its leaves in the rainy season, so it does not shade the crop, and its leaf fall adds organic matter.
**Diversify:** a mix of crops, and small livestock such as goats or poultry whose manure feeds the compost heap, spreads risk if one crop fails.
**Keep soil covered and water stored:** mulch, legumes, pits and tanks are climate-smart because they protect yields in bad years.

blocks.text: Why you need a fair trial

A neighbour says her mulched maize did better. Was it the mulch, or did she also plant earlier, use a new variety and get more rain? The only way to know what works on **your** land is a **side-by-side trial**: two plots, side by side, treated exactly the same except for the one practice you are testing.

items: Choose one change to test, for example mulch versus no mulch.
Mark two plots of the same size, side by side, on similar soil, for example 10 m by 10 m each, with pegs and string.
Use the same variety, planting date, spacing, fertiliser and weeding on both plots.
Label each plot clearly and write the plan in your notebook before planting.
Record observations every week: crop height, colour, wilting in dry spells, pests.
Harvest and weigh each plot separately, then compare per square metre.

blocks.title: One trial season
items: Plan and mark two plots
Plant both the same day
Weekly notes and photos
Harvest and weigh separately
Compare and decide
blocks.caption: Following the same steps every season makes your records comparable from year to year.

blocks.title: Worked example: did the mulch pay?
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa from Module 1 runs a mulch trial on two 100 square metre maize plots. For this example, she values a day of labour at about 3,000 naira and maize grain at about 700 naira per kg; both are approximate and vary by place and season.
steps: Mulched plot: 52 kg of dry grain. Unmulched plot: 40 kg.
Yield per square metre: 52 divided by 100 = 0.52 kg; 40 divided by 100 = 0.40 kg.
Difference: 12 kg more grain, which is 12 divided by 40 = 30 percent more.
Value of extra grain: 12 x 700 = 8,400 naira (approximate).
Extra cost: 1 day collecting and spreading mulch = 3,000 naira (approximate).
Net gain on 100 square metres: 8,400 minus 3,000 = 5,400 naira (approximate).
blocks.result: Mulch paid for itself and more on Hauwa's land this season. Because one season can mislead, she will repeat the trial next year and also watch whether the mulched plot's soil crumbles better at her next soil walk.

blocks.title: Be honest with your numbers
blocks.text: If the result is small, mixed or negative, record it anyway. A dry plot, a cow in the field or late weeding can spoil one plot. Note what happened, repeat the trial, and never stretch one good result into a promise to neighbours.
A simple season record

head: Record
Example entry
rows: Plot B, 10 m x 10 m, mulched
12-day dry spell in July; mulched plot wilted less

takeaways: Climate-smart farming aims at productivity, resilience and lower emissions
Varieties, timing, trees and diversity spread climate risk
A fair trial changes one thing only, on equal plots side by side
Compare yield per square metre and net gain after extra costs
Record every result honestly and repeat before drawing big conclusions

activity.title: Design your trial
steps: Choose the one practice you will test this season
Sketch the two plots with sizes and mark them in the field with pegs
Write your trial plan: what stays the same and what is different
Prepare a season record page with the six rows from the table
Take a dated photo of both plots on planting day
activity.evidence: Your written trial plan, season record page and planting-day photos

lessons.title: Sharing What Works: Extension Services, Farmer Groups and Field Days
objectives: Identify the extension and research services available to you
Make a specific, useful request to an extension officer
Plan and budget a small field day on your trial plots
Explain the costs and options for organic or sustainable claims

blocks.text: Farmers trust what they can see on a neighbour's farm more than what they hear on the radio. Once your trial plots show a difference, they become a teaching tool. This lesson covers who can support you, how to ask for help clearly, and how to share results so other women can copy what works and avoid your mistakes.

blocks.name: teaching
blocks.alt: A woman teaching a small group
blocks.caption: A field day on your own plots can teach more neighbours in one afternoon than months of talk.

blocks.text: Who can support you

head: Partner
What they can offer
How to reach them
rows: Extension officers, training, soil test referrals, information on certified seed
Local Government or zonal ADP office
National Agricultural Extension and Research Liaison Services (NAERLS), Zaria
Extension guides and training materials in several languages
Research institutes and universities, for example IITA in Ibadan
Improved varieties, research results, sometimes demonstration plots
Their websites, field days and partner projects
Shared tools, bulk input buying, labour sharing, learning together
Local leaders, women's associations, church or mosque groups
Training and sometimes inputs for climate-smart or sustainable farming
Ask your ADP which programmes are active in your area

blocks.text: Ask for help in a way that gets results

Extension officers cover many farmers. A vague request such as "help me farm better" is easy to forget. A specific request with your own data is easy to act on. Compare: "My sandy loam field took over an hour to absorb water in the tin test and my maize wilts after one week without rain. Can you advise on a drought-tolerant variety for our zone and visit my mulch trial in July?" Send it with a photo on WhatsApp, then follow up politely if you do not hear back within a week or two.
Learning in groups

The **Farmer Field School** approach, promoted by FAO and many partners, brings a group of farmers together regularly through a whole season on a shared learning plot. They observe the crop, compare practices and decide together, so learning comes from doing rather than lectures. You can use the same idea informally: a group of women from your association meets at your trial plots every two weeks, scouts together, and each tries the practice on a small piece of her own land.

Groups can also solve problems one woman cannot solve alone. Members can take turns helping each other build compost heaps or dig planting pits, which spreads the heavy labour. They can buy a drip kit, a knapsack sprayer with proper protective gear, or certified seed together and share the cost. Agree simple written rules on who keeps shared tools, how they are cleaned, and how costs are split, so friendships survive the season.

blocks.title: A two-hour field day
items: Welcome and the problem
Walk the two plots
Share the numbers
Hands-on practice
Questions and next steps
blocks.caption: Let people see, hear the numbers, then try the practice with their own hands before they leave.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a field day
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi has run a compost and mulch trial on her vegetable plots near Awka and wants to show 15 women from her association. Prices are approximate.
steps: She picks a Saturday afternoon after the market, when most women are free, and allows children to come along with an older girl to mind them.
Budget: drinking water and a small snack, 15 x 500 = 7,500 naira; one-page picture sheet in the local language, 15 x 100 = 1,500 naira. Total 9,000 naira (approximate).
She asks the ADP officer to attend and explain how to get certified seed.
Programme: 15 minutes welcome and the problem, 30 minutes walking the plots, 15 minutes on her numbers, 40 minutes building a small compost heap together, 20 minutes questions.
She collects names and phone numbers, with permission, to start a WhatsApp group for follow-up.
blocks.result: For about 9,000 naira and one afternoon, 15 farmers saw the practice, handled the materials and know whom to ask. Ngozi will record how many try it within the next season.

blocks.title: Protect people's data
blocks.text: Ask before adding anyone to a WhatsApp group or sharing photos of them or their farms. Keep the attendance list safe, and use the group only for farming information that members agreed to receive.
Can sustainable practices earn a better price?

Some buyers, hotels and city customers pay more for produce grown with fewer chemicals, but a claim must be true and checkable. Formal organic certification by an independent body costs money and requires records over several seasons. Some farmer groups use **Participatory Guarantee Systems (PGS)**, a community-based, lower-cost way of checking each other's practices that is recognised by IFOAM - Organics International. Never call produce organic unless you can show it. For finding buyers, grading and pricing, see the WODDI course Agribusiness and Market Access.

takeaways: ADP extension officers, NAERLS, research institutes and farmer groups can all support you
A specific request backed by your own test results gets better help
Field days work best when people see the plots, hear the numbers and try the practice
Organic or sustainable claims must be true and checkable; PGS is a lower-cost option for groups

activity.title: Build your support network
steps: Find the contact for your nearest ADP office or extension officer
Write one specific request using a number from your soil walk or trial
List five women farmers you could invite to see your plots
Draft a simple field day plan with date, programme and approximate budget
activity.evidence: Your written request (or screenshot of it sent), the invitation list and the field day plan

lessons.title: Your Sustainable Farm Project: Evidence, Results and a 90-Day Plan
objectives: Assemble a clear evidence pack from your baseline, practices and trial
Report results honestly, including setbacks and what you would change
Write a 90-day plan with dates, numbers and named partners
Choose indicators to track over the next seasons

blocks.text: This lesson brings everything together into your capstone: a short, honest record of your farm's starting point, the practices you put in place, what happened, and what you will do next. It is written for you first, as a decision tool, and second for anyone you may approach for support, such as an extension officer, a programme or a farmer group.

blocks.name: clipboard
blocks.caption: Your evidence pack turns a season of work into a record you and others can trust.

blocks.text: What goes into your evidence pack

items: **Baseline:** your soil walk table, jar test photo, farm sketch with water sources and the season dates you used
**Practices:** which one or two practices you chose, why, and where on the farm, with dated photos
**Trial and records:** your trial plan, weekly notes and harvest weights for each plot
**Results:** yield per square metre, extra costs and net gain, plus what you observed in dry spells or pest attacks
**Lessons:** what went wrong, what you would change, and what neighbours said
**90-day plan:** your next steps with dates and numbers

blocks.text: Report results honestly

Sustainable practices often show small gains in the first season and larger ones as soil improves. Write what you actually measured, not what you hoped. If a plot was damaged by goats or flooding, say so and explain why the comparison is weaker. A report that says "mulch gave 30 percent more grain this season, but I need a second season to be confident" is more credible and more useful than one that claims a miracle.
Indicators to keep tracking

head: Indicator
How to measure
Good direction
rows: Weigh each plot's harvest and divide by area
Up, or steadier in bad years
Tin test at the same spots each year
Spade block at the same spots and month
Days crop survives a dry spell

blocks.title: Worked example: a project summary
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Jos summarises one season on her 0.25 hectare vegetable and maize farm. Prices are approximate.
steps: Baseline: sandy loam, fast drainage, no dry-season water except a 1,000-litre roof tank; maize yield falling.
Practices: compost on two tomato beds; mulch trial on two 100 square metre maize plots.
Results: mulched maize 0.50 kg per square metre against 0.41 unmulched, which is 0.09 divided by 0.41 = about 22 percent more.
Tomatoes on compost beds needed watering every 3 days instead of every 2 days in the early dry season, saving carrying time.
Setback: one compost heap stayed cold because it was too small; she rebuilt it at 1 m high.
90-day plan: compost on all four beds, share a drip kit with two neighbours, hold one field day, and repeat the mulch trial.
blocks.result: Grace has a one-page summary with clear numbers, an honest setback and a realistic plan that an extension officer or group can support.

blocks.title: Your next 90 days
items: Days 1 to 30: prepare
Days 31 to 60: scale up
Days 61 to 90: share and review
blocks.caption: Break the plan into three months, each with one main goal and a date to check progress.

blocks.text: Writing the 90-day plan

items: Days 1 to 30: prepare materials and land, for example build two new compost heaps and collect mulch.
Days 31 to 60: extend the practice that worked to more of your land, or add a second practice on a trial plot.
Days 61 to 90: share results through a field day or group visit, and review your records against the indicators.
For each step, write the date, the number you aim for (beds, kilograms, people) and the person or partner involved.

blocks.title: Keep it on one page
blocks.text: Most extension officers and programme staff have little time. A one-page summary with a sketch, a small table of numbers and three photos gets read. Keep the full notebook as backup.
If the results disappoint

Not every practice works on every farm in its first season. If your trial showed little or no gain, look for the reason before giving up. Was the mulch too thin, or eaten by termites early? Was the compost still raw when it went on? Did both plots get the same weeding and the same planting date? Did an unusual flood or drought hit one plot harder? Write down your best explanation, adjust one thing, and run the trial again. If a practice still shows no benefit after two fair seasons on your land, it is sensible to drop it and test a different one from your scoring list.

Keep your evidence pack where it is safe from rain and termites, for example in a plastic folder, and back up photos to your phone's cloud storage or send them to yourself on WhatsApp. Records from three or four seasons on the same plots become your most valuable farming asset: they show which practices suit your soil, how your land responds in good and bad years, and they give you credibility when a programme or buyer asks how you farm.

takeaways: Your evidence pack covers baseline, practices, trial records, results, lessons and plan
Honest, measured results build trust and better decisions
Track the same indicators at the same spots and months each year
A 90-day plan needs dates, numbers and named partners

activity.title: Draft your project summary
steps: Gather your baseline sheet, soil walk table, trial plan and season record
Calculate yield per square metre and net gain for your trial plots
Write one paragraph on what went well and one on what went wrong
Write your 90-day plan with three dated steps and numbers
Put it all on one page with up to three photos
activity.evidence: Your one-page project summary with numbers, photos and a dated 90-day plan

quiz.q: Hauwa wants to test mulch. Which trial design is fair?
options: Mulch on a plot planted two weeks earlier with a new variety
Two equal plots side by side, same variety, date and inputs, mulch on one only
Mulch this year on the whole farm and compare with last year's harvest
Mulch on the best soil and no mulch on the worst soil
quiz.explain: A fair trial changes only one thing between equal plots under the same conditions, so any difference is due to the practice.

quiz.q: A mulched plot of 100 square metres gives 45 kg and the unmulched plot gives 36 kg. How much more did the mulched plot yield?
quiz.explain: Difference is 9 kg. 9 divided by 36 = 0.25, which is 25 percent more than the unmulched plot.

quiz.q: Extra grain is worth about 6,000 naira and extra labour for mulching costs about 3,500 naira. What is the approximate net gain?
quiz.explain: Net gain is value of extra harvest minus extra cost: 6,000 minus 3,500 = 2,500 naira.

quiz.q: Which request to an extension officer is most likely to get useful help?
options: Can you give me free fertiliser?
My sandy maize field wilts after a week without rain; which drought-tolerant variety suits our zone, and can you visit my mulch trial in July?
Tell me everything about climate change
quiz.explain: A specific request with her own observations and a clear ask is easy for a busy officer to act on.

quiz.q: Ngozi's group wants to sell vegetables as organic but has no certification. What is the honest approach?
options: Label them organic anyway because they use compost
Explore a Participatory Guarantee System or certification and keep records before making the claim
Say organic only on WhatsApp where nobody checks
Never mention how the vegetables are grown
quiz.explain: Claims must be true and checkable. PGS or certification, backed by records, makes the claim credible.

quiz.q: In the first season, Grace's mulch trial was spoiled when goats ate part of one plot. What should her report do?
options: Report the result, explain the goat damage, and plan to repeat the trial
Estimate what the plot would have yielded and report that as fact
Only report the plot that was not damaged
quiz.explain: Honest reporting includes setbacks and their effect on the comparison. Repeating the trial gives a fairer answer.

finalQuiz.q: Which sign most clearly suggests a field's soil is being run down?
options: Earthworms are common when you dig
Harvest per bag of fertiliser keeps falling in normal-rain years
Water soaks in within a few minutes
finalQuiz.explain: A falling harvest per bag of fertiliser, with normal rain, points to lost organic matter and nutrients. The other options are signs of healthy soil.

finalQuiz.q: A jar test gives sand 4 cm, silt 3 cm and clay 1 cm. What percentage is sand?
finalQuiz.explain: Total is 8 cm. Sand is 4 divided by 8 = 0.5, which is 50 percent.

finalQuiz.q: Which tool helps you plan planting dates for the coming rainy season in Nigeria?
finalQuiz.explain: NiMet's Seasonal Climate Prediction gives expected onset, cessation and season length; combine it with your own rain records.

finalQuiz.q: A farmer with little cash, help two days a week and runoff problems is choosing a first practice. Which scores best on cost, labour and impact?
finalQuiz.explain: Residue mulch costs almost nothing, needs little labour and directly reduces crusting, runoff and moisture loss.

finalQuiz.q: Her compost heap is still cold after two weeks. It is 50 cm high and made only of dry stalks. What should she do?
options: Add greens and manure, moisten it and rebuild to about 1 m high
Leave it uncovered in the sun
Add meat scraps to speed it up
finalQuiz.explain: A heap needs nitrogen-rich greens, moisture and enough size (about 1 m) to heat up. Meat scraps attract animals and should not be added.

finalQuiz.q: Why should tomato not be followed by garden egg on the same plot?
options: They are in the same family and share diseases such as bacterial wilt
Garden egg fixes too much nitrogen
finalQuiz.explain: Tomato, pepper, garden egg and Irish potato belong to one family and share soil-borne diseases, so rotate to another family.

finalQuiz.q: A 40 square metre metal roof receives 30 mm of rain. Using a runoff factor of 0.8, about how much water can be collected?
finalQuiz.explain: 40 x 30 x 0.8 = 960 litres, because 1 mm on 1 square metre gives 1 litre.

finalQuiz.q: Which watering habit is best for vegetables in the dry season?
options: A light splash on the leaves every midday
Deep watering at the base of plants in early morning or late afternoon, after a hand moisture check
Flooding the whole plot daily whatever the soil feels like
Watering only when plants have fully wilted
finalQuiz.explain: Checking moisture and watering deeply at the base in the cool part of the day reduces waste and leaf disease and encourages deep roots.

finalQuiz.q: In push-pull, what is the role of Desmodium planted between maize rows?
options: It attracts pests into the maize
It repels stemborer moths and fall armyworm and suppresses Striga
It is harvested as the main cash crop
It replaces the need for any weeding
finalQuiz.explain: Desmodium pushes pests away and suppresses Striga, while the Napier or Brachiaria border pulls pests out of the crop.

finalQuiz.q: A pesticide label gives a pre-harvest interval of 14 days. She sprayed on 3 August. What is the earliest safe harvest date?
finalQuiz.explain: 3 August plus 14 days is 17 August. Harvesting earlier risks unsafe residues on the food.

finalQuiz.q: In a fair trial, the mulched plot yields 0.48 kg per square metre and the bare plot 0.40 kg. What should she conclude after one season?
options: Mulch gave 20 percent more this season; repeat the trial to confirm
She should stop using fertiliser everywhere
finalQuiz.explain: 0.08 divided by 0.40 = 20 percent more. One season is promising evidence, but repeating the trial confirms it.

finalQuiz.q: Which item belongs in a strong 90-day plan?
options: "By 30 November build two compost heaps; by 15 January hold a field day for 12 women with the ADP officer"
finalQuiz.explain: Good plans have dates, numbers and named partners, so progress can be checked.

capstone.title: Sustainable Farm Practice Project
capstone.brief: A one-page project summary, backed by a notebook evidence pack, showing your farm's soil and water baseline, one or two sustainable practices you implemented, honest trial results with numbers, and a dated 90-day plan to extend the practice and share it locally.
steps: Complete the soil walk at three spots and the farm baseline sheet with water sources and season dates
Choose one or two practices using the cost, labour and impact scoring
Set up a fair side-by-side trial and keep weekly notes and dated photos
Harvest and weigh each plot separately; calculate yield per square metre and net gain
Write what went well, what went wrong and what you would change
Write a 90-day plan with three dated steps, numbers and named partners, and share your results with at least one other farmer or extension officer
evidence: Soil walk table and jar test photo with ruler
Farm sketch with slope, plots and water sources
Practice scoring and chosen practice with reasons
Trial plan, season record and harvest weights for each plot
Calculations of yield per square metre and net gain
Dated photos at planting, mid-season and harvest
